headline_marked: [[1.08 crore Bangladeshis pushed into poverty]] by out-of-pocket medical bills in 2022: Study
headline: 1.08 crore Bangladeshis pushed into poverty by out-of-pocket medical bills in 2022: Study
summary: This figure is nearly double the 56 lakh people affected in 2005, despite a significant drop in the national poverty rate. The study highlights a sharp deterioration in households' ability to afford healthcare.
details: Over 1.08 crore Bangladeshis, or 6.4 percent of the population, were pushed below the poverty line in 2022 due to out-of-pocket (OOP) healthcare expenditure, a new government study has found.

This figure is almost double the 56 lakh people (3.9 percent of the population) pushed into poverty by OOP expenditure in 2005. This rise occurred even as the national poverty rate more than halved from 40 percent in 2005 to 18.7 percent in 2022.

The share of the population facing financial hardship due to healthcare spending also rose significantly, from 28.2 percent in 2005 to 41.7 percent in 2022. This is well above the global estimate of 26 percent.

OOP payments are direct household expenses for healthcare, including medicines, diagnostic tests, and treatment, not covered by government or other sources. A person faces financial hardship when these payments exceed 40 percent of their remaining income after basic needs.

The incidence of catastrophic health expenditure (CHE) climbed from 12.5 percent in 2005 to 32.1 percent in 2022, indicating a sharp deterioration in households’ ability to afford healthcare without financial strain. Average monthly OOP payments (inflation adjusted) rose from Tk 1,241 in 2005 to Tk 3,238 in 2022.

The study, conducted by the Health Economics Unit (HEU) with support from WHO and the Swedish Embassy, identified medicines, diagnostic tests, hospitalisation, and consultation fees as major contributors to these expenses. It also noted a growing reliance on pharmacies for outpatient care, with their share rising from 32.5 percent in 2016 to 55.4 percent in 2022.

The poorest households were disproportionately affected, with 90.8 percent in the lowest consumption quintile facing financial hardship compared to only 13.6 percent in the richest. Rural areas bore the brunt, with 47.9 percent facing hardship compared to 28.2 percent in urban areas.
Barishal division experienced a striking reversal, moving from the lowest rate of financial hardship in 2005 (22.5 percent) to the highest in 2022 (59.1 percent).

The share of public facilities in inpatient care fell from 61.3 percent in 2016 to 56 percent in 2022, while private sector share rose. Concerns were also raised about the distribution of public healthcare benefits, which no longer clearly favored poorer households.

To mitigate financial hardship, the study recommended increasing public financing, improving spending efficiency and equity, restoring pro-poor distribution of public healthcare benefits, ensuring free access to essential medicines and diagnostics, and providing affordable care for chronic conditions.

headline_marked: [[No essential commodity shortages expected before Ramadan]], Minister assures; no immediate edible oil price hike planned.
headline: No essential commodity shortages expected before Ramadan, Minister assures; no immediate edible oil price hike planned.
summary: The Commerce Minister stated sufficient supplies are in the import pipeline to meet demand during Ramadan. He also confirmed no immediate plans to raise edible oil prices.
details: Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir announced yesterday that Bangladesh faces no risk of essential commodity shortages ahead of Ramadan. He also stated there are no immediate plans to increase edible oil prices.

The minister made these remarks in Dhaka after reviewing the supply situation for import-dependent essentials, including edible oil, chickpeas, pulses, and sugar. He confirmed that sufficient quantities are already in the import pipeline to maintain stable supplies.

Despite potential fluctuations in international commodity prices and shipping freight rates, import commitments for key Ramadan items have increased year-on-year. This suggests further support from upcoming shipments.

For instance, edible oil imports rose to 8.23 lakh tonnes from 7.05 lakh tonnes, while sugar imports grew to 6.87 lakh tonnes. Chickpea imports surged significantly to 82,000 tonnes from 12,000 tonnes.

The Bangladesh Trade and Tariff Commission (BTTC) noted that international prices for edible oil and chickpeas remain somewhat elevated, while red lentil prices have declined. The commission recommended close monitoring of global market trends and reviewing tariff structures for sugar and fruit to help stabilize domestic prices.

Muktadir also announced that formal negotiations for a proposed Free Trade Agreement (FTA) with Malaysia have begun. The government aims to conclude these talks and sign the agreement by December 2027.

Discussions on preferential trade arrangements are also underway with other key trading partners, including the UAE, Indonesia, Oman, New Zealand, and the European Union. These agreements are crucial for Bangladesh to retain duty-free and preferential trade benefits after its graduation from the least developed country (LDC) category.
